claim: Blood-sucking insects experience thermal stress at each feeding event on endothermic vertebrates.
source: Blood-sucking insects experience thermal stress at each feeding event on endothermic vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract supported by the study's findings and established knowledge about blood-feeding insects.

claim: During feeding, Rhodnius prolixus sequester and dissipate excess heat in their heads while maintaining an abdominal temperature close to ambient.
source: During feeding, these bugs sequester and dissipate the excess heat in their heads while maintaining an abdominal temperature close to ambient.
evidence: This claim is supported by thermographic data presented in the manuscript showing temperature gradients.

claim: The close alignment of the circulatory and ingestion systems in R. prolixus supports the existence of a countercurrent heat exchanger in the head.
source: The close alignment of the circulatory and ingestion systems, as well as other morphological characteristics, support the existence of a countercurrent heat exchanger in the head of R. prolixus, which decreases the temperature of the ingested blood before it reaches the abdomen.
evidence: This is supported by histological and imaging data showing anatomical relationships.

claim: The countercurrent heat exchanger in R. prolixus decreases the temperature of ingested blood before it reaches the abdomen.
source: The close alignment of the circulatory and ingestion systems, as well as other morphological characteristics, support the existence of a countercurrent heat exchanger in the head of R. prolixus, which decreases the temperature of the ingested blood before it reaches the abdomen.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure and thermographic measurements showing temperature gradients.

claim: This kind of countercurrent heat exchange system has never been described before in the head of an insect.
source: This kind of system has never been described before in the head of an insect.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on literature review.

claim: Countercurrent heat exchange is associated with thermoregulation during blood-feeding in R. prolixus.
source: For the first time, we show that countercurrent heat exchange is associated to thermoregulation during blood-feeding.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Environmental temperature impacts insect body temperature, thus influencing their behaviour and physiology.
source: The entire life of insects highly depends on the environmental temperature (Ta) that impacts their body temperature (Tb), thus influencing their behaviour and physiology.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: Each insect species possesses a temperature range within which individuals can remain active.
source: Each species possesses a temperature range within which individuals can remain active; but within that range, their performance (e.g. food seeking or mating) is still temperature-sensitive (Huey and Stevenson, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Huey and Stevenson, 1979.

claim: At temperatures below or above the activity range, insects can potentially experience thermal stress causing drastic physiological effects and even death.
source: At temperatures below or above the activity range, insects can potentially experience thermal stress causing drastic physiological effects and even death.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect thermal biology.

claim: Different traits have evolved in insects to avoid or minimise the effect of thermal stress due to extreme temperatures.
source: Nevertheless, different traits have evolved to avoid or minimise the effect of thermal stress due to extreme temperatures.
evidence: This is general knowledge about insect adaptations.

claim: Strategies to minimize thermal stress in poikilotherms include behavioural, biochemical, and physiological adjustments.
source: In poikilotherms (i.e. Tb = Ta), these strategies include behavioural (e.g. postural control of exposition to solar radiation), biochemical [e.g. heat-shock proteins (HSPs) synthesis], and physiological (e.g. diapause) adjustments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about thermoregulatory strategies in poikilotherms.

claim: Some insects exhibit morpho-physiological adaptations that allow them to regulate their own body temperature independently of ambient temperature.
source: However, some of them exhibit morpho-physiological adaptations that allow them regulating their own Tb independently of Ta (Heinrich, 1993; May, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Heinrich, 1993 and May, 1979.

claim: Haematophagous insects must expose themselves to high temperatures and their deleterious effects during blood-feeding.
source: If many insect species can avoid thermal stress simply by changing their posture or hide from sun exposure, some others, such as haematophagous (blood-feeding) insects, must expose themselves to high temperatures and their deleterious effects during blood-feeding (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012.

claim: Most haematophagous insects feed on endothermic vertebrates whose blood temperature can be as high as 40°C.
source: Indeed, most of them feed on endothermic vertebrates (e.g. birds) whose blood temperature can be as high as 40°C.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate blood temperature.

claim: Blood-feeding insects must ingest as much blood as possible, as fast as they can, to escape defensive reactions of hosts.
source: On the other hand, in order to escape the defensive reactions of hosts against biting, they must ingest as much blood as possible, as fast as they can.
evidence: This is logical inference about blood-feeding behavior.

claim: Blood-feeding insects must cope with the rapid entry of a large volume of warm fluid, which can generate thermal stress.
source: Thus, they must cope with the rapid entry of a large volume of warm fluid, which temperature (Tblood) can greatly exceeds their own body temperature. This potentially generates thermal stress, and some species respond by synthesising HSPs, a cellular protective mechanism (Benoit et al., 2011; Paim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on HSP synthesis in blood-feeding insects.

claim: Some blood-feeding insect species respond to thermal stress by synthesising heat shock proteins (HSPs).
source: This potentially generates thermal stress, and some species respond by synthesising HSPs, a cellular protective mechanism (Benoit et al., 2011; Paim et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Benoit et al., 2011 and Paim et al., 2016.

claim: Anopheles mosquitoes decrease their abdominal temperature by using evaporative cooling during blood-feeding.
source: For instance, Anopheles mosquitoes decrease their abdominal temperature by using evaporative cooling. They emit through the anus and then keep at the tip of their abdomen a droplet of fluid composed of urine and fresh blood, which evaporates cooling the abdomen, thus reducing the thermal shock and the associated stress caused by the blood-meal (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012.

claim: Anopheles mosquitoes emit a droplet of fluid composed of urine and fresh blood at the tip of their abdomen, which evaporates to cool the abdomen.
source: They emit through the anus and then keep at the tip of their abdomen a droplet of fluid composed of urine and fresh blood, which evaporates cooling the abdomen, thus reducing the thermal shock and the associated stress caused by the blood-meal (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012.

claim: Haematophagous Diptera such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies can obtain a full blood-meal in less than 2 min.
source: Haematophagous Diptera such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies can obtain a full blood-meal in less than 2 min (Lehane, 2005; Lahondère and Lazzari, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lehane, 2005 and Lahondère and Lazzari, 2015.

claim: The duration of exposure to excessive heat is much shorter for Diptera than for kissing bugs.
source: The duration of their exposure to excessive heat is thus much shorter than kissing bugs, for example, that need between 15 and 20 min to feed to repletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the feeding time data presented.

claim: Kissing bugs need between 15 and 20 min to feed to repletion.
source: The duration of their exposure to excessive heat is thus much shorter than kissing bugs, for example, that need between 15 and 20 min to feed to repletion.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about kissing bug feeding behavior.

claim: Kissing bugs can take blood meals that can attain up to 10 times their own unfed weight.
source: Moreover, kissing bugs can take blood meals that can attain up to 10 times their own unfed weight (Lehane, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lehane, 2005.

claim: The heat gain at each feeding event is much higher in bugs than in mosquitoes or flies.
source: So, the heat gain at each feeding event is much higher in bugs than in mosquitoes or flies.
evidence: This is inferred from the larger blood meal size and longer feeding time in bugs.

claim: Heating is deleterious for the physiology of kissing bugs.
source: Interestingly, it has been demonstrated that heating is deleterious for the physiology of kissing bugs.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations to studies on temperature effects.

claim: When kissing bugs are exposed to a sub-lethal temperature of 30°C, they show delayed moulting, sterility and changes in their respiratory metabolism.
source: When they are exposed to a sub-lethal temperature of 30°C, bugs show delayed moulting, sterility and changes in their respiratory metabolism (Okasha, 1968a, Okasha, 1968b, Okasha, 1968c, Okasha, 1968d 1970; Okasha et al., 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Okasha's work from 1968-1970.

claim: Feeding on hot blood induces the synthesis of HSPs in kissing bugs.
source: Feeding on hot blood induces the synthesis of HSPs (Paim et al., 2016), but the increase in their expression level is relatively low compared to other insects (Benoit et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Paim et al., 2016.

claim: The increase in HSP expression level in kissing bugs is relatively low compared to other insects.
source: Feeding on hot blood induces the synthesis of HSPs (Paim et al., 2016), but the increase in their expression level is relatively low compared to other insects (Benoit et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Benoit et al., 2011.

claim: Before blood intake, body temperature equals ambient temperature for all body parts of R. prolixus.
source: Before the blood intake, Tb = Ta for all body parts of the insect.
evidence: This is based on thermographic observations presented in the study.

claim: Once R. prolixus started to feed, different parts of its body did not exhibit the same temperature (heterothermy).
source: But once the insect started to feed, the different parts of its body did not exhibit the same temperature (i.e. heterothermy) (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by thermographic data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: During feeding, the temperature of the proboscis was high and close to the temperature of the blood.
source: Indeed, while the temperature of the proboscis (Tp) was high and close to the temperature of the blood, that of the abdomen (Tabd) was close to the ambient temperature, whereas the temperature of the head (Th) and that of the thorax (Tth) remained intermediate.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: During feeding, the temperature of the abdomen was close to the ambient temperature.
source: Indeed, while the temperature of the proboscis (Tp) was high and close to the temperature of the blood, that of the abdomen (Tabd) was close to the ambient temperature, whereas the temperature of the head (Th) and that of the thorax (Tth) remained intermediate.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: During feeding, the temperature of the head and thorax remained intermediate between proboscis and abdomen temperatures.
source: Indeed, while the temperature of the proboscis (Tp) was high and close to the temperature of the blood, that of the abdomen (Tabd) was close to the ambient temperature, whereas the temperature of the head (Th) and that of the thorax (Tth) remained intermediate.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: A marked thermal gradient was established along the insect body during feeding: Tp >Th > Tth>Tabd.
source: Thus, a marked thermal gradient was established along the insect body: Tp >Th > Tth>Tabd.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: Proboscis and head temperatures oscillated during feeding, in concordance with variations in the activity of the ingestion pumps.
source: Interestingly, Tp and Th oscillated during feeding, certainly in concordance with the variations in the activity of the ingestion pumps, while Tth and Tab did not, remaining stable during the entire blood intake.
evidence: This is based on thermographic observations and inference about pump activity.

claim: Thorax and abdomen temperatures remained stable during the entire blood intake.
source: Interestingly, Tp and Th oscillated during feeding, certainly in concordance with the variations in the activity of the ingestion pumps, while Tth and Tab did not, remaining stable during the entire blood intake.
evidence: This is based on thermographic observations during feeding.

claim: R. prolixus is able to minimise the amount of heat reaching the abdomen during feeding.
source: These results show that R. prolixus is able to minimise the amount of heat reaching the abdomen during feeding (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the thermographic data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: At Ta = 16°C, a clear thermal gradient was observed along the insect bodies when fed on blood at 32°C or 37°C.
source: At Ta = 16°C, we observed a clear thermal gradient along the insect bodies either when fed on blood at 32°C or 37°C (two-way ANOVA, p-values<0.01 for all comparisons, see Table 1, Figure 2C, SI Figure 2—figure supplement 1, SI Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and figures showing temperature gradients.

claim: At Tblood = 37°C and Ta = 16°C, the proboscis was 14°C warmer than the abdomen.
source: At Tblood = 37°C, the proboscis was 14°C warmer than the abdomen.
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the thermographic data.

claim: A temperature gradient between the proboscis and the abdomen was found in insects fed with blood at 32°C, 37°C and 42°C for all the different ambient temperature conditions.
source: A temperature gradient between the proboscis and the abdomen was also found in insects fed with blood at 32°C, 37°C and 42°C for all the different other Ta conditions.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: As ambient temperature increased, body temperature increased in R. prolixus.
source: Moreover, as Ta increased, Tb increased, but we noted that the temperature of the proboscis was more influenced by Tblood, while the abdomen tended to be more stable and did not vary as much, even if the temperature of ingested blood was higher (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements across different ambient temperatures.

claim: The temperature of the proboscis was more influenced by blood temperature than ambient temperature.
source: Moreover, as Ta increased, Tb increased, but we noted that the temperature of the proboscis was more influenced by Tblood, while the abdomen tended to be more stable and did not vary as much, even if the temperature of ingested blood was higher (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of thermographic data across different conditions.

claim: The abdomen temperature tended to be more stable and did not vary as much as other body parts, even when the temperature of ingested blood was higher.
source: Moreover, as Ta increased, Tb increased, but we noted that the temperature of the proboscis was more influenced by Tblood, while the abdomen tended to be more stable and did not vary as much, even if the temperature of ingested blood was higher (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of thermographic data across different conditions.

claim: Different body regions warmed up differentially as a function of both the environment and blood temperatures.
source: Our results showed that the different body regions warmed up differentially as a function of both the environment and blood temperatures (two-way ANOVA, p-values<0.01 for all comparisons, Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) of thermographic data.

claim: The temperature of the proboscis was close to blood temperature, whereas the abdomen remained close to the temperature of the environment.
source: and that the temperature of the proboscis was close to Tblood, whereas the abdomen (Tabd) remained close to the temperature of the environment (Ta).
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: The temperature gradient between proboscis and abdomen was not linear, but exhibited a clear decrease at the posterior region of the head.
source: In between the temperature gradient was not linear, but it exhibited a clear decrease at the posterior region of the head (Figure 2B), revealing that this region is particularly involved in heat transfer.
evidence: This is based on thermographic data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The posterior region of the head is particularly involved in heat transfer.
source: In between the temperature gradient was not linear, but it exhibited a clear decrease at the posterior region of the head (Figure 2B), revealing that this region is particularly involved in heat transfer.
evidence: This is inferred from the temperature gradient pattern observed in thermographic data.

claim: Heterothermy was greatly reduced in insects with severed dorsal vessels compared to intact insects.
source: As a result of the interruption of haemolymph circulation, heterothermy was greatly reduced. The thermal gradient observed was largely reduced in this group of insects (Tp (37.5 ± 0.25°C), Th (36.5 ± 0.33°C), Tth (35.92 ± 0.37°C) and Tabd [35.38 ± 0.32°C]) in comparison to intact insects (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental manipulation and thermographic measurements.

claim: The mean temperature of the proboscis did not statistically differ between dorsal vessel-severed bugs and control bugs.
source: The mean temperature of the proboscis did not statistically differ from control bugs (Student t-test, n = 5, n.s)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Student t-test) of thermographic data.

claim: The temperatures of head, thorax and abdomen regions showed significant differences between dorsal vessel-severed bugs and control bugs.
source: but the comparison of other regions, that is head tip, between eyes, thorax and centre of the abdomen, revealed significant differences (p-values<0.001 in all cases).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of thermographic data.

claim: HSP70 expression was significantly higher in insects with a severed dorsal vessel compared to sham-operated insects.
source: Whereas HSP90 did not evince a significant differential expression, HSP70 expression was significantly higher in insects with a severed dorsal vessel, a condition that impeded countercurrent (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 2, Student t-test p<0.01 two-tailed).
evidence: This is based on qPCR measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: HSP90 did not show significant differential expression between insects with severed dorsal vessel and sham-operated insects.
source: Whereas HSP90 did not evince a significant differential expression, HSP70 expression was significantly higher in insects with a severed dorsal vessel, a condition that impeded countercurrent (Figure 2E, Figure 2—source data 2, Student t-test p<0.01 two-tailed).
evidence: This is based on qPCR measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The head of R. prolixus has a tubular shape, which shrinks a little anteriorly at the basis of the antennae and on its posterior part, just before the thorax.
source: The head of R. prolixus, like other triatomine bugs, has a tubular shape, which shrinks a little anteriorly at the basis of the antennae and on its posterior part, just before the thorax.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations.

claim: The brain is confined to the posterior region of the head in R. prolixus.
source: The brain is confined to the posterior region of the head, whereas the anterior region lodges the large cibarial pump musculature.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: The anterior region of the head lodges the large cibarial pump musculature in R. prolixus.
source: The brain is confined to the posterior region of the head, whereas the anterior region lodges the large cibarial pump musculature.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: There are large areas of haemocoel, both dorsally and ventrally to the nervous system, where haemolymph circulates in R. prolixus.
source: Besides, there are large areas of haemocoel, both dorsally and ventrally to the nervous system, where haemolymph circulates (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Behind the brain, the aorta becomes closely associated with the dorsal wall of the oesophagus.
source: Behind the brain, the aorta (about 170 × 70 µm in section) becomes closely associated with the dorsal wall of the oesophagus (Figure 3B–E, Figure 4C–H).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The aorta is about 170 × 70 µm in section behind the brain.
source: Behind the brain, the aorta (about 170 × 70 µm in section) becomes closely associated with the dorsal wall of the oesophagus (Figure 3B–E, Figure 4C–H).
evidence: This is a measurement from histological sections.

claim: The aorta goes through the brain in close association with the alimentary canal, almost surrounding it.
source: The aorta goes through the brain in the same configuration, almost surrounding the alimentary canal.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: On the anterior part of the head, forward from the optic lobes, the aorta reduces its diameter to about 50–75 µm.
source: On the anterior part of the head, forward from the optic lobes, the aorta reduces its diameter to about 50–75 µm, drops slightly and it turns into an haemolymphatic sinus (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is a measurement from histological sections.

claim: The aorta turns into a haemolymphatic sinus in the anterior part of the head.
source: On the anterior part of the head, forward from the optic lobes, the aorta reduces its diameter to about 50–75 µm, drops slightly and it turns into an haemolymphatic sinus (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: The haemolymphatic sinus is delimited laterally by the muscles of the cibarial pump, ventrally by a thin membrane and dorsally by the head integument.
source: This large sinus is delimited laterally by the muscles of the cibarial pump, ventrally by a thin membrane and dorsally by the head integument (Figure 3B–E, Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The haemolymph that comes from the abdomen, after crossing the brain, is projected in a large space separated from the outside only by the head wall.
source: Consequently, the haemolymph that comes from the abdomen, after crossing the brain, is projected in quite a large space separated from the outside only by the head wall.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure described.

claim: In the head, the alimentary canal is associated with two muscular structures: the cibarial and pharyngeal pumps on the anterior region, and the oesophagus posteriorly.
source: In the head, the alimentary canal is associated with two muscular structures, the cibarial and pharyngeal pumps on the anterior region, and the oesophagus posteriorly (Figures 5,6).
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: On the anterior region of the head, the cavity of the cibarial pump is a flattened U-shaped structure of about 150 µm large, running medially.
source: On the anterior region of the head, the cavity of the cibarial pump is a flattened U-shaped structure of about 150 µm large, running medially (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a measurement and description from histological sections.

claim: The muscles of the cibarial pump are voluminous, occupying much of the anterior part of the head.
source: The muscles of the cibarial pump are voluminous, occupying much of the anterior part of the head (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The oesophagus consists of a cylindrical tube of about 50 µm diameter that extends to the thorax.
source: The oesophagus consists of a cylindrical tube of about 50 µm diameter that extends to the thorax (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a measurement from histological sections.

claim: The circulatory system and the alimentary canal are in close contact almost throughout the length of the head.
source: The circulatory system and the alimentary canal are in close contact almost throughout the length of the head (Figures 3, 4C–H).
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In some areas, the aorta surrounds lateral parts of the oesophagus making their contact even more intimate.
source: Moreover, transverse sections highlight that in some areas, the aorta surrounds lateral parts of the oesophagus (Figure 4F–G) making their contact even more intimate.
evidence: This is based on histological observations shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Only thin layers of cells composing the walls of the aorta and the oesophagus separate the two cavities.
source: Only thin layers of cells composing the walls of the aorta and the oesophagus separate the two cavities.
evidence: This is based on histological observations.

claim: The dorsal vessel is open at its anterior part and the circulation of haemolymph is postero-anterior in insects.
source: As in other insects, the dorsal vessel is open at its anterior part and the circulation of haemolymph is postero-anterior.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect circulatory systems.

claim: The abdominal part of the dorsal vessel is attached to the dorsal diaphragm, which delimits the visceral and the pericardial sinuses.
source: The abdominal part of the dorsal vessel is attached to the dorsal diaphragm, which delimits the visceral and the pericardial sinuses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect circulatory anatomy.

claim: The dorsal vessel bends down anteriorly just before entering the thorax.
source: The dorsal vessel bends down anteriorly just before entering the thorax.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations.

claim: In R. prolixus, all the ostia (four pairs) and alary muscles are grouped in a small section of the vessel, at the terminal segments of the abdomen.
source: In R. prolixus, in contrast to most insect species, all the ostia (four pairs) and alary muscles are grouped in a small section of the vessel, at the terminal segments of the abdomen (Chiang et al., 1990), that is where the haemolymph remains the coolest during the feeding process (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 1990 and thermographic data.

claim: The location of ostia in R. prolixus is where the haemolymph remains the coolest during the feeding process.
source: In R. prolixus, in contrast to most insect species, all the ostia (four pairs) and alary muscles are grouped in a small section of the vessel, at the terminal segments of the abdomen (Chiang et al., 1990), that is where the haemolymph remains the coolest during the feeding process (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is based on thermographic data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: At the level of the head, the haemolymph warms up by conduction due to the close contact between the aorta and the oesophagus containing the ingested blood, which circulates in the opposite direction.
source: At this level, the haemolymph warms up by conduction due to the close contact between the aorta and the oesophagus containing the ingested blood, which circulates in the opposite direction (anterior-posterior) (Figures 4, 5).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure and thermographic observations.

claim: The cibarial pump works as a piston, producing a pulsed wave of blood towards the gut.
source: First, the cibarial pump works as a piston, producing a pulsed wave of blood towards the gut.
evidence: This is based on X-ray imaging observations.

claim: The pharyngeal pump shows a pulsed activity at the same frequency as the cibarial pump, but in an opposite phase.
source: Second, the small pharyngeal pump, barely considered in the literature about kissing bugs, also shows a pulsed activity, at the same frequency, but in an opposite phase to the pharyngeal pump (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is based on X-ray imaging observations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: R. prolixus possesses anatomical specificities and adaptations that allow this species to minimize the heat transfer to its abdomen.
source: Here, we have shown that R. prolixus also possesses anatomical specificities and adaptations that allow this species to minimize the heat transfer to its abdomen, thus reducing the heat shock associated with feeding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined anatomical and thermographic data.

claim: While the head is the most exposed to heat during feeding, the amount of heat reaching the thorax and the abdomen is dramatically reduced.
source: While the head is the most exposed to heat, the amount of heat reaching the thorax and the abdomen is dramatically reduced.
evidence: This is based on thermographic measurements during feeding.

claim: Anatomically, the structures in R. prolixus conform to a countercurrent heat exchanger between the alimentary canal and the circulatory system.
source: Anatomically, the structures conform to a countercurrent heat exchanger between the alimentary canal and the circulatory system.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical observations and functional analysis.

claim: In the countercurrent heat exchanger, cool haemolymph coming from the end of the abdomen withdraws heat from the just ingested blood that is flowing into the alimentary canal in the opposite direction.
source: In the area where the aorta is in close contact with the oesophagus, cool haemolymph coming from the end of the abdomen withdraws heat from the just ingested blood that is flowing into the alimentary canal in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on anatomical structure and thermographic data.

claim: The haemolymph flows in the semi-open space (haemolymphatic sinus) and bathes the warm muscles of the ingestion pump.
source: Then, the haemolymph flows in the semi-open space (i.e. haemolymphatic sinus) and bathes the warm muscles of the ingestion pump.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations.

claim: In the anterior part of the head, the haemolymph circulates in close contact with the body wall, releasing heat towards the environment.
source: Finally, in the anterior part of the head, the haemolymph is conducted to project through the haemocoel, thus circulating in close contact with the body wall, releasing heat towards the environment (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure and thermographic observations.

claim: The continuous flow of both fluids is required for an efficient heat exchange.
source: The continuous flow of both fluids is required for an efficient heat exchange.
evidence: This is a general principle of countercurrent heat exchange.

claim: The coordinate action of the two ingestion pumps (cibarial and pharyngeal), which contract in opposite phase, results in a continuous flow of warm blood to the gut.
source: This appears to be assured by the coordinate action of the two ingestion pumps, that iscibarial and pharyngeal, which contraction on opposite phase results in a continuous flow of warm blood to the gut, resembling the Windkessel effect of the vertebrate aorta (See SI Video 1).
evidence: This is based on X-ray imaging observations and inference.

claim: The coordinate action of the ingestion pumps resembles the Windkessel effect of the vertebrate aorta.
source: This appears to be assured by the coordinate action of the two ingestion pumps, that iscibarial and pharyngeal, which contraction on opposite phase results in a continuous flow of warm blood to the gut, resembling the Windkessel effect of the vertebrate aorta (See SI Video 1).
evidence: This is an analogy drawn from the observed pump activity.

claim: The peristaltic contracting waves of the dorsal vessel maintain continuous flow of cool haemolymph in the opposite direction to blood flow.
source: On the other hand, the peristaltic contracting waves of the dorsal vessel do the same with the cool haemolymph, but in the opposite direction.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of insect circulatory physiology.

claim: The close contact between the aorta and the oesophagus facilitates the exchange of heat, which returns to the head.
source: The close contact between the aorta and the oesophagus facilitates the exchange of heat, which returns to the head.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure and thermographic observations.

claim: Only a relatively small amount of heat leaves the head during feeding.
source: Consequently, only a relatively small amount of heat leaves the head (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on thermographic observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: By sequestering the heat in the head, the countercurrent heat exchanger allows the insect to minimise heat transfer to the thorax and the abdomen, thus maintaining a regional heterothermy.
source: In this way, by sequestering the heat in the head, this countercurrent heat exchanger allows the insect to minimise heat transfer to the thorax and the abdomen, thus maintaining a regional heterothermy (Figure 2).
evidence: This is the main conclusion about the function of the countercurrent heat exchanger.

claim: Countercurrent heat exchangers are present in some insect species, where they modulate the flow between the thorax and the abdomen, of heat excess produced by the activity of flight muscles.
source: Countercurrent heat exchangers are present in some insect species, where they modulate the flow between the thorax and the abdomen, of heat excess produced by the activity of flight muscles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect thermoregulation.

claim: In Cuculiinae winter moths, two heat exchangers are localised in the thorax and at the junction between the thorax and the abdomen.
source: In Cuculiinae winter moths, two heat exchangers are localised in the thorax and at the junction between the thorax and the abdomen. These exchangers enable these insects to fly at very low Ta by sequestering heat in their thorax. Air sacs also help to restrain heat propagation to the abdomen (Heinrich, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1987.

claim: Heat exchangers in winter moths enable these insects to fly at very low ambient temperature by sequestering heat in their thorax.
source: These exchangers enable these insects to fly at very low Ta by sequestering heat in their thorax. Air sacs also help to restrain heat propagation to the abdomen (Heinrich, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1987.

claim: Air sacs help to restrain heat propagation to the abdomen in winter moths.
source: Air sacs also help to restrain heat propagation to the abdomen (Heinrich, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1987.

claim: In bumblebees, the heat exchanger is located in the narrow passage of the petiole and helps them to exchange heat via the haemolymph between the thorax and the abdomen.
source: In bumblebees, the exchanger is located in the narrow passage of the petiole and helps them to exchange heat via the haemolymph between the thorax and the abdomen (Heinrich, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1976.

claim: Xylocopa carpenter bees produce endogenous heat during flight.
source: As in previous examples, Xylocopa carpenter bees produce endogenous heat during flight.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carpenter bee physiology.

claim: The countercurrent exchanger in Xylocopa carpenter bees occurs in the petiole area where the aorta presents many loops thus facilitating heat dissipation via the abdomen.
source: The countercurrent exchanger occurs in the petiole area where the aorta presents many loops thus facilitating heat dissipation via the abdomen (Heinrich and Buchmann, 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich and Buchmann, 1986.

claim: Robber flies (Diptera: Asilidae) use their abdomen as a heat dissipater.
source: Robber flies (Diptera: Asilidae) also use their abdomen as a heat dissipater (Morgan and Shelly, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Morgan and Shelly, 1988.

claim: Anatomical particularities help insect species to maintain a regional heterothermy.
source: All these anatomical particularities help these insect species to maintain a regional heterothermy, and has been speculated that this could protect critical organs (e.g. gonads) from an eventual thermal stress due to extreme temperature, keeping others (e.g. muscles) at optimal higher temperatures.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the function of heat exchangers in insects.

claim: Regional heterothermy could protect critical organs (e.g. gonads) from thermal stress due to extreme temperature, keeping others (e.g. muscles) at optimal higher temperatures.
source: and has been speculated that this could protect critical organs (e.g. gonads) from an eventual thermal stress due to extreme temperature, keeping others (e.g. muscles) at optimal higher temperatures.
evidence: This is presented as speculation about the adaptive value of regional heterothermy.

claim: The heat-exchange system of R. prolixus is unique in that it is located in the head and is involved in the management of the heat flow derived from food intake.
source: The heat-exchange system of R. prolixus is unique, in the sense that it is located in the head and that it is involved in the management of the heat flow derived from the food intake.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding compared to other known heat exchangers.

claim: Countercurrent heat exchangers occur in vertebrates such as birds, fishes, and mammals.
source: Countercurrent heat exchangers are not restricted to invertebrates, they also occur in vertebrates such as birds (Arad et al., 1989), fishes (Carey et al., 1971; Stevens et al., 1974), and mammals (Scholander and Schevill, 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on vertebrate heat exchangers.

claim: In vertebrates, heat transfer occurs between arteries reaching zones of potential heat loss and veins carrying cold blood, in order to recuperate heat back to the body core or to active muscles.
source: In these animals, heat transfer occurs between arteries reaching zones of potential heat loss (e.g. appendices) and veins carrying cold blood, in order to recuperate heat back to the body core (e.g. artic birds and mammals) or to active muscles (e.g. fishes).
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate countercurrent heat exchange.

claim: The heat exchanger found in the head of R. prolixus is associated with other features that facilitate heat dissipation during feeding, such as the elongated form of the head.
source: The heat exchanger found in the head of R. prolixus is associated to other features that facilitate heat dissipation during feeding, as the elongated form of the head, which increases the surface/volume ratio and the relatively glabrous cuticle, typical of hemipterans.
evidence: This is inferred from morphological observations.

claim: The elongated form of the head increases the surface/volume ratio in R. prolixus.
source: The heat exchanger found in the head of R. prolixus is associated to other features that facilitate heat dissipation during feeding, as the elongated form of the head, which increases the surface/volume ratio and the relatively glabrous cuticle, typical of hemipterans.
evidence: This is a basic geometric principle applied to the observed morphology.

claim: R. prolixus has a relatively glabrous cuticle, typical of hemipterans.
source: The heat exchanger found in the head of R. prolixus is associated to other features that facilitate heat dissipation during feeding, as the elongated form of the head, which increases the surface/volume ratio and the relatively glabrous cuticle, typical of hemipterans.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and knowledge of hemipteran characteristics.

claim: Bumblebees show a regional difference in depth of insulation: the regions where heat needs to be stored are densely piled whereas the ventral part of the abdomen, which serves as a thermal radiator, is completely free of hair.
source: For instance, bumblebees show a regional difference in depth of insulation: the regions where heat needs to be stored are densely piled (thorax, dorsal part of the abdomen) whereas the ventral part of the abdomen, which serves as a thermal radiator, is completely free on hair (Heinrich, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1976.

claim: In some syrphid flies that produce heat endothermically with thoracic muscles, the removal of hair from the thorax leads to an increase of the cooling rate of about 30% compared to hairy flies of the same species.
source: In some syrphid flies that produce heat endothermically with thoracic muscles, the removal of hair from the thorax leads to an increase of the cooling rate of about 30% compared to hairy flies of the same species (Heinrich, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1987.

claim: Winter moths that need to keep heat to be able to fly in the cold maintain a high thoracic temperature and minimise heat loss by means of a thick insulated pile.
source: Winter moths that need to keep heat to be able to fly in the cold maintain a high thoracic temperature and minimise heat loss by means of a thick insulated pile (Heinrich, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Heinrich, 1987.

claim: The heart of R. prolixus is unusual in that all eight ostia are grouped in a short section at the very end of the abdomen (segment VII).
source: Moreover, the heart of R. prolixus is unusual in that all eight ostia are grouped in a short section at the very end of the abdomen (segment VII) (Chiang et al., 1990), where the temperature of the haemolymph is the coolest (Figure 2A and B) inside the insect body.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chiang et al., 1990 and thermographic data.

claim: In other Hemiptera species, ostia are grouped at the posterior region of the abdomen.
source: In other Hemiptera species, ostia are grouped at the posterior region of the abdomen (Hinks, 1966).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hinks, 1966.

claim: In the haematophagous bugs R. prolixus and Triatoma infestans, ostia are located in the terminal part of the abdomen, grouped in the VII and VIII abdominal segments.
source: In the case of the haematophagous bugs R. prolixus and Triatoma infestans, they are located further in the terminal part abdomen, grouped in the VII and VIII abdominal segments (Hinks, 1966; Barth, 1980; Chiang et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hinks, 1966; Barth, 1980; and Chiang et al., 1990.

claim: Stomoxys calcitrans has three pairs of ostia which span five abdominal segments.
source: For instance, Stomoxys calcitrans has three pairs of ostia which spanned five abdominal segments (Cook and Meola, 1988)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cook and Meola, 1988.

claim: In Anopheles gambiae, haemolymph enters the heart through six pairs of incurrent abdominal ostia and one pair of ostia located at the thoracic-abdominal junction.
source: and in Anopheles gambiae hemolymph enters the heart through six pairs of incurrent abdominal ostia and one pair of ostia located at the thoracic-abdominal junction (Glenn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Glenn et al., 2010.

claim: Bugs eliminate drops of urine during feeding, similar to mosquitoes.
source: It is worth mentioning also that, as mosquitoes, bugs eliminate drops of urine during feeding (SI Video 1).
evidence: This is based on video observations.

claim: The size and time that urine drops remain attached to the tip of the abdomen in bugs are both reduced compared to mosquitoes.
source: Although the size and the time that these drops remain attached to the tip of the abdomen are both reduced, and evaporative cooling is hardly probable to occur as in Anopheles (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012)
evidence: This is based on observations and comparison with mosquitoes.

claim: Evaporative cooling is hardly probable to occur in bugs as in Anopheles.
source: Although the size and the time that these drops remain attached to the tip of the abdomen are both reduced, and evaporative cooling is hardly probable to occur as in Anopheles (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012)
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that drops are smaller and remain for less time.

claim: Urine drops may reduce the temperature of the terminal part of the abdomen, precisely in the area where the haemolymph enters the heart.
source: these drops may reduce the temperature of the terminal part of the abdomen, precisely in the area where the haemolymph enters the heart to be pulsed forwards.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible function of the urine drops.

claim: The aorta is open on its dorsal part in the cephalic portion and goes through the cibarial pump muscles.
source: The aorta is open on its dorsal part in the cephalic portion and goes through the cibarial pump muscles.
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations.

claim: The warmed haemolymph is poured around the cibarial pump muscles that are also warmed by both contractions and direct contact with the alimentary canal which contains the circulating warm blood.
source: The warmed haemolymph is thus poured around these muscles that are also warmed by both contractions and direct contact with the alimentary canal which contains the circulating warm blood.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical structure and thermographic observations.

claim: The wide sinus, in which the insect haemolymph circulates in contact with the insect integument, probably facilitates heat loss by convection and radiation.
source: The wide sinus, in which the insect haemolymph circulates in contact with the insect integument, probably facilitates heat loss by convection and radiation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the anatomical structure.

claim: Two tracheas extend along the head, next to both the pharyngeal pump and the alimentary canal.
source: Finally, two tracheas extend along the head, next to both the pharyngeal pump (Figure 3C–D) and the alimentary canal (Figure 4C–D, SI Video 3 and SI Video 4) (Ramírez-Pérez, 1969).
evidence: This is based on anatomical observations and a citation.

claim: Tracheas may help decrease the temperature of the head by circulating air and by internal evaporative cooling.
source: These tracheas may also help decrease the temperature of the head by circulating air and by internal evaporative cooling.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible function of the tracheas.

claim: Internal evaporative cooling is a common strategy in species, such as plant juice feeders, which can obtain water easily.
source: Internal evaporative cooling is a common strategy in species, such as plant juice feeders (Prange, 1996), which can obtain water easily.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prange, 1996.

claim: In the tsetse fly Glossina morsitans, a decrease of 2°C of the body temperature occurs when the ambient temperature exceeds the thermal upper limit of tolerance thanks to evaporation via the spiracles.
source: In the tsetse fly Glossina morsitans, a decrease of 2°C of the Tb occurs when the Ta exceeds the thermal upper limit of tolerance thanks to evaporation via the spiracles (Edney and Barrass, 1962).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Edney and Barrass, 1962.

claim: The process of evaporative cooling via the ventilatory system is documented in grasshoppers and beetles with a decrease of the body temperature up to 8°C.
source: The process of evaporative cooling via the ventilatory system is also documented in grasshoppers and beetles with a decrease of the Tb up to 8°C (Prange, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Prange, 1990.

claim: In R. prolixus during feeding, there is an increase in the rate of exchange of CO2, O2, and water vapour, thought to be linked with spiracle opening.
source: In R. prolixus during feeding, there is an increase in the rate of exchange of CO2, O2, and water vapour: this is thought to be linked with spiracle opening (Leis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leis et al., 2016.

claim: If heat loss via the trachea occurs in R. prolixus, it could resemble respiratory countercurrent mechanisms found in the nose of mammals, birds, and reptiles.
source: If the hypothesis of heat loss via the trachea is true in R. prolixus, it could resemble to respiratory countercurrent mechanisms found in the nose of mammals, birds, and reptiles. In these animals, the heat exchanger cools the blood flowing to the brain to reduce overheating (Tattersall et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism, with a citation for comparison.

claim: In mammals, birds, and reptiles, the heat exchanger in the nose cools the blood flowing to the brain to reduce overheating.
source: In these animals, the heat exchanger cools the blood flowing to the brain to reduce overheating (Tattersall et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tattersall et al., 2006.

claim: Until now, the only thermoregulatory mechanism associated with blood-feeding known in insects was evaporative cooling performed by Anopheles mosquitoes.
source: Until now, the only thermoregulatory mechanism associated with blood-feeding known in insects, was evaporative cooling performed by Anopheles mosquitoes (Lahondère and Lazzari, 2012).
evidence: This is a claim about the state of knowledge before this study, supported by a citation.

claim: The work on R. prolixus revealed a new original mechanism of thermoregulation, based on morphological and physiological specific adaptations.
source: Our work in R. prolixus not only unravelled a new species possessing thermoregulatory abilities, suggesting that it may be also present in other haematophagous insects, but also revealed a new original mechanism, based on morphological and physiological specific adaptations.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: Thermoregulatory abilities may be present in other haematophagous insects besides R. prolixus.
source: Our work in R. prolixus not only unravelled a new species possessing thermoregulatory abilities, suggesting that it may be also present in other haematophagous insects
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in R. prolixus.

claim: It is possible that countercurrent heat exchangers could be more frequent and diversified than commonly thought.
source: It is possible that countercurrent heat exchangers could be more frequent and diversified than commonly thought.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discovery of a new type of heat exchanger.
